title: What a chart can tell me
text: A chart makes some patterns easier to see, but it also reflects a series of choices. Which observations belong in the plot? What belongs on each axis? Which differences deserve attention?

title: What a chart can tell me
text:
One choice that matters
In a comparison of income and life expectancy, a logarithmic income axis changes the spacing of the values. That can help reveal patterns that are difficult to see when a few large values stretch the scale.

title: What a chart can tell me
section: What I still need to ask
text:
What I still need to ask
A visible association does not explain why the pattern exists. Before moving from description to explanation, I need to think about the research question, the data, and possible alternative explanations.
My next step is to describe the plot in one careful sentence, then write down a question it cannot answer.

title: Doctors, ugh!
text:
After far too long, I finally figured out my health insurance situation so it was high time that I actually put medical to use. I was feeling lousy all week and since I missed a few days of classes, the wolves were at my door and I needed a doctors note.
I went to a clinic nearby and it was smooth getting in. Once I was in the check-up room I made some small talk with the technician, asking how they liked their job. The tech offered to let me do my own Covid test and I obliged remarking that I had plenty of experience during the pandemic swabbing my own nose.
Some time passed and my tests came back negative for Covid and Influenza and the PA came in to ask me some questions, check my lungs with the stethoscope and looked down my gullet for strep. Even with all that, she couldn’t figure out what was making me feel so ill. As she was halfway out the door to get some more tests, she asked me if I needed a doctors note. The tone of her voice harmonized with the look on her face that sang the melody that was on my mind. I nodded, she winked and stepped out of the room.
A nurse came in shortly thereafter and told me she needed to swab my throat. I said of course and let her go about her business. This nurse shoved the swab all the way to my uvula which made me gag hard enough that I could see her wince as she pulled the swab out. We both connected over a hearty chortle and we were both on our way out.
I left feeling a mix of accomplishment and dissatisfaction with the fact that they couldn’t figure out what my exact ailment was. But one thing is certain: I got my damn doctor’s note.

text:
This website begins with a simple idea: make a little space for work that is still taking shape.
Not every post needs to be a finished argument. I want to use this notebook to explain something I’ve learned, record a question that stayed with me, or connect an idea from class to something I noticed elsewhere.

title: Academic interests & research
text:
I landed into Political Science because I was having numerous debates with friends who held all sorts of political beliefs and my most convincing arguments were arguments backed by statistics. However, statistics can never tell the full story.
I am really interested in people’s lived experiences in the world that we live in and I want to help tell those stories.

Individuals: Who are the people we live around and what shapes their experiences?
Cities and communities: How do local environments shape everyday choices?
Film and communication: How can I make a film both meaningful and easy to understand?

A project I’m helping develop

The Race Project
IDEPENDENT PROJECT · IN PROGRESS
Question. How do people view and understand race and racism?
Approach. Dr. Julius Doyle and I film interviews with people and ask them questions regarding their thoughts and feelings on race and racism.
What I’m learning. I am learning that what people have to say on this topic will always surprise you. With every person I interview, my own ideas are challenged. Read a reflection on this project
